disposition_reason: A methods-comparison study of portable XRF and a diphenylcarbazide colorimetric test against ICP-MS for detecting lead chromate adulteration in spices. The 69 spice samples were drawn from a larger library to span a wide lead range, so the Table 1 lead summaries describe a purposive method-test set, not occurrence in a market or a finished food.
disposition_locator: Abstract; Spice Sample Selection, p. 16997; Table 1, p. 16998

study.design: Analytical method comparison (pXRF, DPC colorimetric assay, ICP-MS) on a purposive spice set
study.origin: India (Patna), Pakistan, Bangladesh, Republic of Georgia
study.market: markets and homes (field library), as stated
study.period_text: Patna, India samples 2020; Pakistan roots 2019; Bangladesh roots 2017; Georgia samples 2019
study.method: pXRF (Olympus Vanta C) in collection bags; ICP-MS (Thermo XSERIES 2) after microwave nitric acid digestion; DPC colorimetric test for Cr(VI)
study.lod_text: pXRF about 2 mg Pb/kg for spice powders; ICP-MS limit not given for this study (0.001 mg/kg quoted from prior work)
study.qa: Triplicate digestions; at least three blank digestions per 30 samples; spike tests for the colorimetric assay; ICP-MS used as reference in lieu of CRMs

regulatory_or_exposure.what: WHO/FAO maximum lead limit in consumable salts (quoted)
National lead standards for turmeric powder, Bangladesh and India (quoted)
New York City reference lead limit applied to spices (quoted)

unresolved: Table 1 prints ICP-MS lead summaries by spice type (for example all samples n = 69, mean 1075, median 137, maximum 11,531 mg/kg; Indian red chili powder n = 10, mean 114 mg/kg). Per the owner's instruction these are not recorded as occurrence findings because the samples were selected to span a lead range for method testing.
Per-sample values are in Supporting Information Table S1, which is not in the filed PDF.
